The countries that oppose Russia’s participation in world sports disregard the principles of the Olympic Charter, said President Vladimir Putin at a meeting of the Council for the Development of Physical Culture and Sports. He said that Russia is in contact with many national federations. According to him, federations in a number of countries refuse to play matches with Russia under pressure from their governments. "But what does this indicate? It indicates that those who are fighting for uniform rules and for the maintenance of democratic institutions themselves disregard all these rules and these institutions. Unfortunately, these are the people we have to deal with on the international stage," the president said. "We need to continue following this legal path, to uphold the decisions, including those of the Court of Arbitration for Sport, because they are disregarding the judicial system in this area and, in fact, are disregarding all the principles of the Olympic International Charter."

headlines.full_text: Putin vows to keep pursuing Russia's interests in world sports The head of state said that countries which oppose Russia’s involvement in world sports are disregarding the principles of the Olympic Charter MOSCOW, November 12. /TASS/. Russia will continue to consistently work to safeguard its interests in the international sports arena, President Vladimir Putin told a meeting of the Council for the Development of Physical Culture and Sports. He said that countries which oppose Russia’s involvement in world sports are disregarding the principles of the Olympic Charter. "In general, they are simply again demonstrating that there are no universal rules - there are only those rules that meet their interests," Putin said. "We must consistently and calmly pursue our interests. And that is what we will do in all areas."
headlines.llm_reasoning: The piece frames Russia's sports involvement as a defense of national interests, portraying opponents as violating Olympic principles.

headlines.full_text: The Fallout From the Fall of Jensen Huang Export controls can be tightened, but don’t hurt American AI. Jensen Huang’s resignation Thursday as the rock-star CEO of Nvidia was necessary following reports that he had affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate. But it also does regrettable harm to the company and America’s AI industry, and maybe that was China’s plan. Nvidia’s stock price dropped 4.3% on Thursday after Mr. Huang announced his resignation. The company has lost $500 billion in market value in a week and nearly $1.5 trillion in the last month. Lesson: Never put too much money in one stock—or too much stock in one CEO. Mr. Huang has been a charismatic evangelist for AI and helpfully pushed back against the doomers. His inspiring story of founding Nvidia as a Taiwanese immigrant at a Denny’s some three decades ago is a welcome antidote to attacks on America’s capitalist system. America’s AI dominance owes in part to Mr. Huang. Nvidia designs the world’s most advanced AI chips and has used its balance sheet to finance dozens of startups, sometimes through deals that give customers money to buy its chips. But its cozy relationships with customers also may have made it vulnerable to Chinese subterfuge, as Mr. Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang lays bare. Ms. Huang founded the Singapore-based cloud provider Megaspeed, which bought high-end Nvidia chips and rented out computing capacity in Southeast Asia to Chinese firms. His successor has the toughest job in tech A company built around one man must now learn to run without him TWO OF THE world’s most valuable companies have changed bosses in recent months. They could hardly have done so more differently. At Apple, Tim Cook made way for John Ternus in September under what the iPhone-maker called a “long-term succession plan”. Nvidia’s succession plan lasted four days. Jensen Huang, the chip giant’s only boss in its 33-year history, never intended to leave. On November 8th he confessed to an affair; on November 12th, after further revelations about his private life, he resigned. The job has fallen, for now, to Colette Kress, Nvidia’s finance chief since 2013, who has been named interim chief executive. She was never coached for the top job, and will need to learn fast. Since news of the scandal broke Nvidia’s shares have lost about 20% of their value (see chart). Besides calming investors, she will need to shore up suppliers, mend fences with Washington and hold together the vast web of financing schemes and partnerships that has fuelled Nvidia’s breakneck growth. Ms Kress inherits one of the most formidable money-making machines in corporate history. Two-thirds of the world’s artificial-intelligence computing power runs on Nvidia’s chips. Its gross margins hover around 75%, against 55% at AMD, a rival chip designer. This financial year analysts expect it to bring in more than $400bn in revenue, nearly double last year’s total. headlines.full_text: Clashes erupt in Barcelona after thousands join Spain general strike Tens of thousands of people have been taking part in the strike, called by the country's main unions over housing and the high cost of living. Clashes have broken out between groups of masked men and police in Barcelona after tens of thousands of people took part in Spain's first general strike for 14 years, called by the country's main unions over housing and the high cost of living. Some 120,000 people joined a demonstration in the capital Madrid and more than 50,000 turned out in Barcelona, where footage showed masked men setting fire to rubbish bins and smashing shop windows as police fired tear gas. Transport and other public services across Spain faced serious disruption. Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November. The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant." There was a heavy police presence in the centre of Barcelona on Wednesday evening, with officers wearing helmets and riot shields. Some of the disturbances took place in the Passeig de Gràcia, close to the iconic Plaça de Catalunya in the centre of the city. Small fires burned in the middle of the streets as bins were set alight. Local media reported that a group of people fired fireworks towards police and looted shops including the Lego store. Protesters were also seen trying to enter the Apple Store. The BBC spoke to a woman who attended the protests in Barcelona who said it was mostly very peaceful and "joyful". headlines.full_text: ‘Labelled terrorists’: How France is using anti-terror powers to deter protests The French government has been accused of weaponising an anti-terror law adopted in the wake of the 2015 Paris attacks to keep dozens of people away from massive protests sweeping the country. Lawyers and rights groups denounce an abuse of power with potentially dangerous repercussions for individual liberties and the right to protest. The French government has been accused of weaponising an anti-terror law adopted in the wake of the 2015 Paris attacks to keep dozens of people away from massive protests sweeping the country. Lawyers and rights groups denounce an abuse of power with potentially dangerous repercussions for individual liberties and the right to protest. Issued on:12/11/2026 - 18:32Modified:12/11/2026 - 18:38 The protestsroiling Franceover the past two months have seen hundreds of thousands of demonstrators march in towns and cities across the country, exercising a cherished right to voice discontent overunderfunded schools, the cost of living andpolice brutality. Some, however, have been stripped of that right, in the name of the fight against terror. After peaceful rallies gave way to widespreadrioting and looting on October 17, the government began using special anti-terror powers to bar several dozen people from attending further demonstrations – without prior approval from judges. They included students, trade unionists, far-left activists and environmental campaigners with no criminal record, most of whom had never been investigated forterrorism. It marked the largest use of such discretionary powers since the2024 Olympic and Paralympic Gamesin Paris, when more than 500 people were ordered to stay home or barred from getting anywhere near the venues, leading several tolose their jobs. For lawyers, unions and rights groups, it also marked a turning point in the policing of protest movement

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says her government will come up with "sector-specific" advice to help those facing this kind of threat. Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threats on Wednesday, too. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected. On Thursday morning, a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed international and national train services in northern France. The latest incidents follow a series of bomb hoaxes last week against airports and airlines in a number of European countries. When a sand dune collapses onto a tent sheltering displaced Palestinians, killing four children and a woman, it is tempting to describe the tragedy as another consequence of winter storms. But there is nothing natural about a catastrophe in which people have been driven from their homes, denied the means to rebuild them and left to face freezing temperatures under pieces of canvas. The rain may have triggered the collapse, but the conditions that made it deadly were created by a human-made siege. Behind these tragedies lies a reality that no humanitarian statement can adequately capture: families who survived bombardment are now struggling to survive the cold, flooding and collapsing ground. They escaped Israeli attacks only to find themselves exposed to another form of danger. For the fourth consecutive winter, Palestinians are being forced to endure conditions that no civilian population should be expected to survive. The first major winter storm reportedly flooded around 70,000 tents within approximately twelve hours. Humanitarian organizations estimate that Gaza needs between 200,000 and 300,000 new tents or caravans to provide displaced families with even basic protection. headlines.full_text: Five new miniature frog species found in eastern Himalayas Scientists say the frogs evolved as the Himalayas rose and the Asian monsoon took shape. Scientists have discovered five new species of tiny horned frogs in India's eastern Himalayas, more than doubling the number of known species in the group. A team of scientists from University of Delhi and Harvard University made the discoveries after five years of fieldwork, identifying the frogs as members of the Jingophrys group. Among them is Jingophrys tanogogo - or the snail-eating horned frog - the first frog known in India to feed on snails and the first member of its family recorded with such a diet. The research suggest the Himalayas have played a much larger role in frog evolution than previously thought and highlight the region as an overlooked hotspot for biodiversity. The Himalayas, stretching from tropical forests to alpine meadows, are among the world's richest biodiversity regions. headlines.full_text: National diabetes week highlighting prevention, early detection TEHRAN – The health ministry is observing national diabetes week from November 11 to 17 to raise public awareness of the disease and highlight the importance of prevention and early diagnosis in its effective management. TEHRAN – The health ministry is observing national diabetes week from November 11 to 17 to raise public awareness of the disease and highlight the importance of prevention and early diagnosis in its effective management. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), diabetes is a chronic disease that occurs either when the pancreas does not produce enough insulin or when the body cannot effectively use the insulin it produces. Insulin is a hormone that regulates blood glucose. Hyperglycaemia, also called raised blood glucose or raised blood sugar, is a common effect of uncontrolled diabetes and over time leads to serious damage to many of the body’s systems, especially the nerves and blood vessels. Currently, more than 588 million people aged 20–79 years are living with diabetes, and the figure is projected to exceed 852 million by 2050. In addition, some 252 million individuals are not aware of their conditions yet. Based on the results of the eighth national survey of non-communicable diseases (NCD) risk factors, carried out in Iranian year 1400 (2021-2022), at least 14 percent of the population aged above 25, equal to 7.5 million people, suffer from diabetes, the health ministry’s website quoted Jafar Jandaghi, an official with the health ministry, as saying. When including those with prediabetes, impaired glucose tolerance, the total number reaches 20 million, he added. Mamdani pledged to dismantle the NYPD’s Strategic Response Group (SRG) during his 2025 mayoral campaign following accusations that its officers had used excessive force against protesters. headlines.full_text: Still haven't filed your taxes? Here's what you need to know So far this tax season, the IRS has received more than 90 million income tax returns for 2022. So far this tax season, the IRS has received more than 100 million income tax returns for 2022. That means tens of millions of households have yet to file their returns. If yours is among them, here are some last-minute tax-filing tips to keep in mind as the Tuesday, April 18 deadline approaches. Not everyone has to file on April 18:If you live in a federally declared disaster area, have a business there — or have relevant tax documents stored by businesses in that area — it’s likely the IRS has already extended the filing and payment deadlines for you.Hereis where you can find the specific extension dates for each disaster area. Thanks to many rounds of extreme weather in recent months, for instance, tax filers in most of California — which accounts for 10% to 15% of all federal filers — have already been granted an extension until Oct. 16 to file and to pay, according to an IRS spokesperson. If you’re in the armed forces and are currently or were recently stationed in a combat zone, the filing and payment deadlines for your 2022 taxes are most likely extended by 180 days. But your specific extended filing and payment deadlines will depend on the day you leave (or left) the combat zone.This IRS publicationoffers more detail. Taxes and adulting: What to know about filing taxes on your own for the first time Lastly, if you made little to no money last year (typically less than $12,950 for single filers and $25,900 for married couples), you may not be required to file a return.

headlines.full_text: Retail spending fell in March as consumers pull back Spending at US retailers fell in March as consumers pulled back amid recessionary fears fueled by the banking crisis. Spending at US retailers fell in March as consumers pulled back after the banking crisis fueled recession fears. Retail sales, which are adjusted for seasonality but not for inflation, fell by 1% in March from the prior month, the Commerce Department reported on Friday. That was steeper than an expected 0.4% decline, according to Refinitiv, and above the revised 0.2% decline in the prior month. Investors chalk up some of the weakness to a lack of tax returns and concerns about a slowing labor market. The IRS issued $84 billion in tax refunds this March, about $25 billion less than they issued in March of 2022, according to BofA analysts. That led consumers to pull back in spending at department stores and on durable goods, such as appliances and furniture. headlines.full_text: Iran designates Argentine navy and air force as terrorist organizations TEHRAN – Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has designated the Argentine Navy and Air Force as terrorist organizations in response to Buenos Aires’ decision to designate the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization. TEHRAN – Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has designated the Argentine Navy and Air Force as terrorist organizations in response to Buenos Aires’ decision to designate the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization. In a statement issued on Wednesday, the ministry said the measure was taken in accordance with the principle of reciprocity and under Iran’s 2019 law on reciprocal action against the US designation of the IRGC as a terrorist organization. The statement described Argentina’s decision as a hostile act that violates fundamental principles of international law, emphasizing that the IRGC is an integral branch of Iran’s official Armed Forces. It cited the 2019 legislation, which stipulates that any country that, in any manner, follows or supports the United States’ decision to designate the IRGC as a terrorist organization is subject to reciprocal action. “Accordingly, the Argentine Navy and the Argentine Air Force are subject to the provisions of the aforementioned law and are hereby designated as terrorist organizations,” the statement said. The ministry added that the Argentine government would bear full responsibility for all consequences arising from the measure.
headlines.llm_reasoning: The article portrays Argentina’s navy and air force as terrorists in retaliation for their designation of the IRGC, blaming them for hostile actions.

headlines.full_text: COP 31: UN launches $3 billion disaster financing platform, brings together its six agencies The UN Disaster Risk Financing Platform aims to make financing more predictable, allowing governments and humanitarian agencies to act ahead. The United Nations on Thursday launched a new disaster risk financing platform at COP31 in Turkey's Antalya, aiming to secure access to more than $3 billion to protect 75 million people and their livelihoods from climate shocks by 2030. Bringing together six UN agencies, the initiative seeks to address a major gap in humanitarian response. Less than 2% of global humanitarian financing is currently arranged in advance, leaving agencies heavily dependent on funds mobilised after disasters strike. The UN Disaster Risk Financing Platform aims to make financing more predictable, allowing governments and humanitarian agencies to act ahead of floods, droughts, storms and other extreme weather events, rather than waiting for a crisis to unfold. It will bring together the expertise and data of the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), the International Organisation for Migration (IOM), the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), UNICEF, the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and the World Food Programme (WFP). It will also work with insurance companies and financial markets to expand access to pre-arranged financing and reduce the cost of such interventions. Middletown, Tinton Falls, Red Bank, Keansburg, Lincroft and North Middletown may see flash flooding.
